title: THE HIDDEN BOTTLENECK OF AI
subtitle: WHY NVIDIA CAN'T EXIST WITHOUT SK HYNIX

scenes.narration: Forty thousand dollars buys Nvidia's most powerful AI accelerator. It packs two hundred and eight billion transistors into a package the size of a dinner plate. But without a small stack of memory built in Icheon, South Korea, that chip is dead silicon. The memory is HBM. The supplier is SK Hynix. And the reason Nvidia cannot simply buy it elsewhere is a story about physics, packaging, and a narrow chokepoint in modern industry.

The stakes are clear. Every Blackwell rack needs enormous amounts of high bandwidth memory, and the supply is not elastic. SK Hynix says its HBM capacity sold out well before the year began, and warns shortages could persist to the end of the decade. When a component is booked years in advance, memory stops being a part. It becomes the schedule. That schedule runs through a handful of fabs in one country.

Engineers call the gap between compute and memory the memory wall. For decades, caches and prefetching hid it. Artificial intelligence broke the illusion. A large model streams billions of parameters through the chip for every token, and the arithmetic units wait for data. The GPU is no longer the scarce resource. The scarce resource is the path that feeds it. That path begins with a memory architecture called HBM.

Start with the graphics card you know. A gaming GPU sits next to a handful of GDDR chips. They are cheap, dense, and fast when traffic is light. Each bit travels across copper traces on a printed circuit board, and every trace must arrive at the same instant. At multi gigabit speeds, a few millimetres of extra length is not a detail. It is a timing error. The board itself becomes the limit.

Those traces behave like transmission lines. They have capacitance, inductance, and resistance. High frequency signals leak, reflect, and interfere with their neighbours. The further a bit travels, the more energy it burns and the more it distorts. Engineers add layers, better substrates, and shielding. But every fix costs power and board area. You can only push a signal across copper so far before the physics stops cooperating.

Then there is the energy bill. Moving one bit across a wire costs energy, and the cost rises with distance and speed. On a graphics card, that energy becomes heat. Multiply it by hundreds of billions of bits per second, and cooling becomes a design constraint. Data centres pay for that heat twice, once at the wall socket and again at the cooling plant. The industry calls this energy per bit. That is the hidden cost.

The memory wall is measurable. Over two decades, floating point throughput grew far faster than the bandwidth of ordinary memory. Caches absorbed the traffic for general computing. Artificial intelligence is different. Matrix multiplication is insatiably hungry for data. An arithmetic unit with no data is an expensive heater. A GPU with enough compute but not enough bandwidth sits idle, and idle silicon still draws power. That is the economic definition of a bottleneck.

Modern language models make the problem worse in two directions. Training reads enormous datasets and repeatedly touches the same weights. Inference reads the entire model for every token, plus a growing key value cache. Both care about capacity as much as bandwidth. A GPU with too little memory cannot hold the model. A GPU with too little bandwidth cannot keep its cores busy. You need both, in a package that fits on a server board.

So why not bolt more GDDR onto the board. The answer is pin count, board area, and power. Each chip needs its own data lanes, power delivery, and share of the thermal budget. A processor can only drive so many high speed pins before the package becomes impractical. Widen the bus, and the traces get longer and the signal integrity gets worse. The architecture runs into a wall made of copper, not ambition.

The way out was to stop treating memory as a board-level part. Put it directly on the processor package. Stack the memory dies vertically, connect them with microscopic vias, and join the stack to the GPU through a silicon interposer. That idea became high bandwidth memory. The distance collapses from centimetres to millimetres, and the energy cost collapses with it. But the stack creates a new problem. How do you build it without destroying yield.

Inside the stack, the dies are connected by through silicon vias, or TSVs. These are microscopic holes drilled through each memory die and filled with copper. Thousands run vertically through the stack, carrying power, data, and control signals. The dies must be thinned to a fraction of a millimetre, aligned with micron precision, and bonded without cracking. One bad via can ruin an entire stack. Every extra layer multiplies the risk.

The stack then sits on a silicon interposer, a piece of silicon that acts like a miniature motherboard. The interposer carries thousands of fine traces between the GPU and the memory stacks. This is called two point five D packaging, because the chips sit side by side. It is expensive, difficult, and the only practical way to deliver enough bandwidth. The interposer, not the transistor, became the bottleneck.

High bandwidth memory evolved through several generations. The first arrived in twenty thirteen. HBM2 doubled the stack height and data rate. HBM2E added twelve high stacks. HBM3 pushed one stack past eight hundred gigabytes per second. Then HBM3E arrived with a twelve high stack, thirty six gigabytes, and one point two terabytes per second. Each generation demanded thinner dies, more vias, and better packaging. Packaging became the hard part.

HBM3E is the generation that powered Nvidia's Blackwell accelerators. A twelve high stack holds thirty six gigabytes and delivers about one point two terabytes per second. Nvidia pairs four to eight stacks around the GPU. Total bandwidth reaches eight terabytes per second on a flagship part. That is ten times a consumer graphics card, in a package that fits on a server board. But stacking eight around one die is a packaging nightmare.

Stacking that many dies creates three problems at once. The first is thickness. To keep the package within a fixed height, each die must be thinned as more layers are added. The second is warpage. Thin silicon bends under heat and pressure, and a bent stack will not bond reliably. The third is heat. Every die generates power, and that heat must escape through the same narrow path. The taller the stack, the worse all three become.

The conventional way to hold the stack together is thermal compression non conductive film, or TC-NCF. A film of adhesive is placed between each layer, then heat and pressure bond the stack. Samsung and Micron stayed with film. SK Hynix used it too, through the second generation of HBM. But the film sits between the silicon and the heat spreader, adding thermal resistance exactly where heat needs to escape. At twelve layers, yield collapses.

SK Hynix's alternative was mass reflow molded underfill, or M R MUF. Instead of a film between every layer, the entire stack is reflowed at once and filled with a liquid epoxy molding compound. The epoxy flows into the gaps and around the bumps, then hardens into a solid protective layer. Because it fills the stack, it conducts heat better and spreads stress more evenly. SK Hynix also added up to four times more thermal dummy bumps.

beats.label: Yield gauge 70% SK hynix vs competitor

scenes.narration: The results were measurable. SK Hynix says its first M R MUF process improved heat dissipation by thirty six percent. For twelve high HBM3, it developed advanced M R MUF, with a new molding compound offering one point six times the heat dissipation. The process gave better warpage control and reduced pressure on each die. By HBM3E mass production, SK Hynix reported yields of seventy percent.

That yield number is the heart of the story. A memory stack is useless if only half the finished units work. Nvidia needs millions of stacks, on schedule, reliable for years in a data center. SK Hynix could deliver them at volume. Samsung struggled with heat and yield on early HBM3E. The result was not a permanent monopoly, but close enough. Nvidia gave the largest share to the supplier that could actually ship.

Here is the allocation that makes the chokepoint visible. TrendForce and Korean media reported that Nvidia's first HBM4 volume split gave SK Hynix the mid fifty percent range, Samsung the mid twenty percent range, and Micron around twenty percent. That is not a textbook monopoly. It is a chokehold. The largest customer cannot diversify faster than its second supplier can fix yield. And that is exactly what Samsung set out to do.

The irony is that SK Hynix nearly went bankrupt before the boom. In twenty twenty three, the memory market collapsed. Prices fell, inventories piled up, and the company reported an operating loss of more than seven point seven trillion Korean won. It was the kind of year that forces a memory maker to retreat. SK Hynix did the opposite. It kept betting on high bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, and the idea that AI would eventually need far more memory.

The bet paid off faster than expected. In twenty twenty four, SK Hynix reported an operating profit of twenty three point five trillion won. In twenty twenty five, operating profit nearly doubled to forty seven point two trillion won, on revenue of ninety seven trillion won. High bandwidth memory grew into more than forty percent of its DRAM revenue. A commodity cyclical became the most profitable supplier in the AI supply chain.

High bandwidth memory is also a different business from ordinary DRAM. It consumes at least twice the wafer capacity of standard memory for the same output, because of stacking and packaging. Every bit of HBM displaces two bits of commodity DRAM. When demand surges, supply cannot respond quickly. Fabs take years to build, and packaging lines take months to qualify. The result is pricing power commodity memory never enjoyed, and a shortage downstream.

Geography amplifies the concentration. SK Hynix produces DRAM in Icheon and Cheongju, South Korea. Its newest fab, M15X in Cheongju, represents an investment of more than twenty trillion won and is designed to ramp HBM capacity. A much larger cluster is rising in Yongin, with a first fab targeted for twenty twenty seven. Advanced packaging lines are being added in Cheongju and Indiana. A single disruption here can move the entire AI roadmap.

There is a second chokepoint, and it is not in Korea. The GPU and its memory stacks are assembled on a silicon interposer through CoWoS. That process belongs to TSMC. Starting with HBM4, the memory's base die is also built on a logic process, which brings TSMC deeper into memory. Nvidia can design the accelerator, but it cannot ship it without Korean memory and Taiwanese packaging. Every side of this triangle is a bottleneck.

Samsung did not stand still. By twenty twenty six, reports put its HBM4 yield near eighty percent, up from below sixty percent at the start of mass production. It combined sixth generation DRAM with a four nanometre logic die and pushed data rates higher. That is a real comeback. But it arrived after years of yield learning, and Nvidia had already locked in volume. The lead is not permanent, but it is expensive to erase.

Now the next generation is here. HBM4 doubles the interface from one thousand and twenty four bits to two thousand and forty eight bits. It supports sixteen stacked dies, thirty six gigabytes at twelve high and forty eight gigabytes at sixteen high, and delivers around two terabytes per second per stack. SK Hynix completed development first and is ramping production for Vera Rubin. The bandwidth doubles again, and so does the packaging difficulty.

Beyond HBM4, the industry is preparing to remove the solder bumps entirely. The technique is called hybrid bonding. Instead of connecting chips through microscopic solder balls, hybrid bonding presses two surfaces together so copper pads fuse directly to copper. The pitch shrinks from around twenty microns to below one micron. That means more connections, shorter paths, less heat, and sixteen or more dies. SK Hynix has already validated twelve high hybrid bonding.

But hybrid bonding is not a free lunch. Copper expands when heated, and the surfaces must be almost perfectly flat and clean. A single particle can create a void across an entire interface. The equipment is expensive and the yield curve is steep. That is why the industry is delaying the transition where it can. The physical limit is no longer the transistor. It is the wire, the bump, the adhesive, and the heat.

Solving the memory stack moves the bottleneck again. The GPU, the HBM stacks, and the base die must be assembled on a silicon interposer, and that interposer is getting larger and more expensive. TSMC's CoWoS capacity is finite. A single large package can consume an entire production slot, and yield falls as the interposer grows. Nvidia can design the chip, and SK Hynix can build the memory. But without enough advanced packaging, neither can ship.

There is also a materials layer that almost nobody sees. The most advanced lithography depends on photoresists from a handful of Japanese suppliers, including JSR, Tokyo Ohka, and Shin-Etsu. Those chemicals help pattern the logic and memory die. A disruption in Japan, a fire in a single plant, or an export control can ripple through Korea and Taiwan. The AI supply chain is not a triangle. It is a stack of dependencies.

That is the real lesson. The AI boom is usually told as a story about compute. But every leap in compute exposes a new physical limit somewhere else. Moving memory onto the package solved bandwidth, but created a packaging bottleneck. Stacking more dies solved capacity, but created a heat and yield problem. Hybrid bonding solves the solder bump, but creates a cleanliness and copper expansion problem. Each answer becomes the next question.

The companies that win are not always the ones with the best chip. They are the ones that control the physical path between compute and data. Nvidia designs the brain. SK Hynix builds the memory that feeds it. TSMC packages the two together. Japanese chemical makers supply the materials for patterning.  That is why a memory company in Korea can hold leverage over the most valuable chip company in the world.

And that is where the story turns. Solving HBM4 with hybrid bonding does not end the bottleneck. It moves the constraint to advanced packaging, where interposer size, CoWoS capacity, and materials purity decide how fast AI can scale. The next episode follows that trail. How TSMC's packaging lines and Japan's photoresists became the quiet gatekeepers of the AI boom. The memory wall is behind us. The packaging wall is next.
